# Annual Career Review System

## Why This Matters
Career growth is a compound system. Better decisions early reduce switching costs and improve long-term optionality.

## Practical Framework
1. Define one 12-month target role with explicit success criteria.
2. Build a capability backlog across knowledge, projects, and collaboration behavior.
3. Run 4-week execution sprints and collect measurable evidence.
4. Review outcomes quarterly and adjust strategy using market and fit signals.

## Implementation Checklist
- Clear role target and industry context
- Evidence-based skill gap map
- Portfolio or project proof
- Feedback loop with mentors and stakeholders

snapshot.title: Annual Career Review System
snapshot.excerpt: Use the work, feedback, and constraints you already have to decide what to continue, change, or stop—and turn that decision into a realistic next step.
snapshot.body_md:
# Annual Career Review System

An annual career review should end with a decision about how you will spend your next working year. A useful result might be to stay and negotiate different responsibilities, develop a missing capability, explore another employer, or reduce commitments that you cannot sustain.

Start with evidence from the year you actually had. You do not need a new career goal, another assessment, or a perfect record before you begin.

This guide helps you turn existing materials into three outputs: a short account of what changed, a choice between realistic options, and a next action with a review point. The tables are practical editorial tools, not a scored assessment or a predictor of career success.

## Reconstruct the year before judging it

Open your calendar, project folders, completed work, and feedback. Include more than the most recent success or difficult week.

Choose examples from different parts of the year: work that went well, work that stalled, ordinary recurring responsibilities, and something you stopped doing. Record what the materials establish and where they leave uncertainty.

For each significant piece of work, answer:

- What problem were we trying to solve?
- What did I personally decide, produce, or coordinate?
- What happened, and how do I know?
- What depended on other people or conditions?
- Would I want to do more of this work under similar conditions?

“Completed the reporting project” says little about your contribution. “Defined the reporting requirements, reconciled conflicting definitions with two teams, and documented the agreed process” identifies actions you can discuss and potentially repeat.

Separate three kinds of statement:

| Kind of statement | Example | How to use it |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Observation | Two colleagues used the procedure I wrote | Evidence that the work was used |
| Interpretation | The procedure may have made handovers clearer | A plausible explanation to check |
| Unknown | I do not know whether errors fell | A gap, rather than an achievement to claim |

You can still make decisions with incomplete evidence. Keep the uncertainty visible instead of filling it with confidence.

## Look across contribution, development, and conditions

Reviewing output alone can miss an unsustainable workload. Reviewing feelings alone can miss useful capabilities acquired during a difficult project.

Use these questions to examine both:

| Area | Question | Materials to consult |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Contribution | What useful work did I help deliver? | Completed work, decisions, feedback, operational records |
| Capability | What can I now do with less help or in a more demanding situation? | Earlier and later work samples, review comments |
| Task interest | Which activities would I choose to repeat? | Notes made during projects, examples from different periods |
| Working conditions | What helped or hindered good work? | Schedules, interruptions, staffing, access to support |
| Practical options | What choices are feasible now? | Relevant vacancies, internal opportunities, available time and resources |

Look for patterns without turning them into permanent labels. Enjoying one analysis project is a reason to investigate similar work. It does not establish that every analytical role will suit you.

If you already use a RIASEC report, compare its interest descriptions with the tasks you actually experienced. The [RIASEC PDF and download guidance](/en/holland-test/pdf-download) is available for report-related questions. Interest results describe interests; they do not establish skills, qualifications, or the career you should choose.

UCSF’s career reflection guidance encourages returning to what you have learned, your interests, values, and skills, and keeping dated records so you can notice change. Its original audience is graduate students and postdoctoral researchers; here, that principle is adapted into a review of work evidence. [UCSF reflection guidance](https://career.ucsf.edu/gsp/career-exploration/reflection).

## Identify the decision that matters now

Finish this sentence:

> Because this year showed ______, I need to decide whether to ______.

Examples include:

- Because my strongest work involved investigating problems, I need to decide whether to seek more analytical responsibilities.
- Because delivery depended on repeated evening work, I need to decide which commitments to renegotiate.
- Because I want to change industries, I need to decide which missing requirement to investigate first.

Then compare options that you could genuinely take. Include a reasonable version of staying: different responsibilities, clearer priorities, or a time-limited development opportunity. Compare that with an external move or another route where relevant.

Do not average away a condition you cannot accept. A role offering interesting work may still be infeasible if its location, schedule, or entry requirements conflict with your circumstances.

| Option | Evidence supporting it | Important uncertainty | Cost or constraint | Next check |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Stay with revised responsibilities |  |  |  |  |
| Seek an internal move |  |  |  |  |
| Explore another employer or field |  |  |  |  |

The strongest next step is often the one that answers the uncertainty most likely to change your choice. If staying depends on access to a particular project, discuss that access before committing to a large training plan.

## Worked example: deciding whether to stay

The following is a fictional teaching example. The person, documents, discussions, and observations are invented.

Maya is a project coordinator. She starts her review thinking, “I worked hard but went nowhere, so I should leave.”

She gathers a project calendar, three completed project summaries, a procedure she wrote, review comments, and her own notes about working hours.

The materials show different things:

| Material | What Maya can reasonably conclude | What it does not establish |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Two completed handover projects | She coordinated dependencies and maintained delivery records | That she caused every positive project outcome |
| A procedure used by another team | Her documentation was usable beyond her own work | That it produced a measured productivity gain |
| Comments requesting clearer analysis | Explaining conclusions is a development need | That she lacks analytical potential |
| Repeated evening work around changing requests | The current way of handling changes needs attention | That every coordinator role has the same conditions |

Maya notices that she enjoyed clarifying confusing processes but disliked repeatedly chasing late inputs. Leaving remains an option, but the evidence suggests a more specific question: can she obtain work that includes process investigation while reducing routine chasing?

She compares staying unchanged, negotiating a revised assignment, and exploring external roles. Staying unchanged would preserve the problem. An immediate external search would not tell her whether the task mix was actually different.

She therefore proposes a bounded internal trial: investigate one recurring handover problem, produce a recommendation, and have a manager review her reasoning. She also asks which existing responsibility will be reduced so the trial fits within her working time.

In the fictional discussion, the manager agrees to the project and names a reviewer but initially offers no workload adjustment. Maya changes the proposal before accepting it: a smaller investigation replaces one recurring reporting task.

At the review point, she will examine whether the work happened, whether her analysis improved after feedback, and whether the workload arrangement held. She will not judge the trial solely by whether a promotion followed.

Her decision rules are explicit:

- If the assignment and workload adjustment happen, complete the trial and review the work.
- If the assignment exists but feedback is unavailable, agree a reviewer before extending it.
- If the work never becomes available, use that evidence to reconsider an internal or external move.
- If the arrangement repeatedly requires unacceptable working hours, revisit its scope rather than adding more commitments.

The review has changed a broad judgment about her career into a testable choice about her next assignment.

## Turn the choice into a small commitment

Write the action, the support needed, and the point at which you will decide what follows.

The University of Edinburgh’s annual review guidance for researchers connects reflection with realistic objectives, development support, and progress conversations during the year. Its institutional provisions are specific to Edinburgh; the transferable lesson here is to agree how an objective will be supported and reviewed. [Edinburgh annual review guidance](https://support-for-researchers.ed.ac.uk/career-development/annual-review-guidance-for-researchers).

Copy this closing note:

> **My main finding:**  
> **What I will continue:**  
> **What I will change or stop:**  
> **The next action:**  
> **Support or agreement required:**  
> **Evidence I expect to have afterward:**  
> **Review date or event:**  
> **What would make me continue, adjust, or choose another option:**

Do not invent an outcome target when the first task is to learn. “Obtain feedback on a completed recommendation” is a clearer commitment than promising a business improvement you cannot yet estimate.

## When the review does not produce a clear answer

If records are sparse, start with the materials available and seek specific feedback on a recent piece of work. Do not reconstruct a confident twelve-month story from one conversation.

If feedback conflicts, ask what each person observed and what standard they used. Different responsibilities can produce different judgments.

If every option has a drawback, distinguish a temporary compromise from a condition you cannot accept. A temporary choice needs a reason and a review point.

If circumstances require action sooner—such as a confirmed role ending—use the review to identify usable evidence and immediate constraints. You do not need to finish an elaborate annual exercise first.

When you have chosen a direction, use [Build a Five-Year Career Roadmap](/en/career/guides/build-five-year-career-roadmap) to connect the next step with later possibilities. If the immediate problem is demonstrating your work, go to [Build a Portfolio for Career Switching](/en/career/guides/build-portfolio-for-career-switch). The [career guides library](/en/career/guides) provides other starting points.

Your review is complete when you can explain the choice, the evidence behind it, and what you will check next.

snapshot.title: Build a Five-Year Career Roadmap
snapshot.excerpt: Connect a long-term direction to practical stages, evidence of readiness, and clear conditions for changing course—without pretending you can predict your next five job titles.
snapshot.body_md:
# Build a Five-Year Career Roadmap

A five-year career roadmap connects the work you want to move toward with the capabilities, experience, and conditions needed to get there.

Its useful detail changes with distance. Your next project can be specific. A possible role several years away should remain a hypothesis until you know more about its work and requirements.

The result should help you answer two questions: “What should I do next?” and “What would make me change this route?”

## Describe the work before choosing the title

Write a direction statement that includes the problem you want to work on, the people or organisations you hope to serve, and the conditions that matter.

For example:

> I want to help organisations make better operational decisions by investigating problems, working with data, and explaining recommendations. I need a route that lets me remain employed while I develop those capabilities.

This statement leaves room for several job titles. It also gives you something to compare with actual work.

A direction such as “become a director” leaves essential questions unanswered. Do you want responsibility for people, budgets, technical decisions, or a wider programme? Which of those activities have you experienced?

Use current job descriptions and relevant official career profiles to identify actual responsibilities. Record the location, date, and role level. A small set of vacancies can reveal requirements to investigate; it cannot establish the whole market or predict demand five years from now.

## Establish your starting position

Before adding courses, list what you can already do and the evidence behind it.

| Starting point | What to record |
| --- | --- |
| Relevant work | Tasks completed, level of independence, difficulty, feedback |
| Development needs | Tasks you cannot yet perform or explain adequately |
| Access | Projects, equipment, data, supervision, or training you can realistically obtain |
| Constraints | Available time, location, caring responsibilities, income requirements |
| Formal requirements | Qualifications or registration to verify for the exact role and jurisdiction |

Keep interest separate from readiness. Wanting more investigative work is useful information, but it does not establish that you can yet perform a target role. If you use a RIASEC report, the [PDF and download guidance](/en/holland-test/pdf-download) can help with report-related questions; use the report alongside task experience rather than as a qualification.

Harvard Graduate School of Design’s individual career planning worksheet brings together existing skills, development needs, interests, personal circumstances, support, and goals. It was written for graduate students. This guide adapts those planning questions for people designing a route through work and learning. [Harvard GSD career planning worksheet](https://www.gsd.harvard.edu/wp-content/uploads/2021/10/Careers-in-Focus-Worksheet-1.pdf).

## Divide the route by changes in responsibility

A stage should describe a meaningful change in what you can do. Time provides a planning boundary; it does not prove readiness.

A route might move through:

- Trying representative tasks with guidance.
- Completing a bounded piece of work independently.
- Handling a more complex problem with several stakeholders.
- Taking responsibility for a larger area or helping others deliver it.

These are examples, not a universal progression. A regulated occupation may require a defined educational and supervised route. Another role may develop through employment and projects. Check the responsible local regulator or official training authority where formal requirements apply.

For each stage, identify an output, a standard, and a dependency.

“Finish a course” is an activity. “Produce an analysis that answers a defined question, document the method, and resolve substantive reviewer comments” describes evidence of capability.

Passing an editorial milestone does not establish professional qualification or entitlement to promotion. Its purpose is to inform your next planning decision.

## Worked roadmap: from coordination toward operational analysis

This is a fictional teaching example. The person, assignments, feedback, and changes described below are invented.

Noor coordinates service requests. She wants more analytical responsibility but has not yet completed an analysis from question definition to recommendation.

Her starting materials are a reporting spreadsheet she maintains, feedback showing that she communicates clearly, and a calendar indicating that she can protect a modest amount of development time. She cannot use confidential workplace data outside authorised work.

She drafts this route:

| Planning period | Development question | Evidence to produce | Dependency | Condition for the next stage |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| First six months | Do I understand and enjoy the core analytical tasks? | A small project using synthetic or appropriately licensed public data | Time to practise and someone able to review the method | Can explain the question, cleaning choices, findings, and limitations |
| Remainder of year one | Can I apply the method to a bounded operational problem? | An authorised project with a clear brief and feedback | Access to a suitable assignment and reviewer | Can complete the agreed work with an appropriate level of support |
| Year two | Can I handle a less structured question? | A comparison of options, assumptions, and a recommendation | Experience with relevant tools and the organisation’s processes | Reasoning stands up to challenge and important uncertainties are visible |
| Years three to five | What level and type of responsibility should I pursue? | Evidence from progressively more demanding work | Suitable opportunities, sustained interest, and feasible conditions | Choose a specialist, broader operational, or other route using experience |

The later rows deliberately do not promise a job title. Noor has not yet experienced enough of the work to decide whether she wants technical depth, wider business responsibility, or people management.

### What happens when the first stage exposes a gap?

In the fictional first project, Noor produces a clear chart but cannot explain why some records were excluded. Her reviewer asks whether the result would change if the exclusions were handled differently.

The project has answered part of the development question: she enjoys investigation, but her data decisions need work. Noor does not solve this by adding a new certificate to the roadmap. She revises the project brief to include an exclusion log and a comparison of results under different assumptions.

She then reviews the revised work against the same question. The adjustment is tied to an observed gap.

### What happens when the planned opportunity disappears?

Later, the workplace assignment is cancelled. That does not show Noor is incapable of analysis. It removes a dependency.

She considers three routes:

1. Find another authorised internal assignment.
2. Continue a clearly labelled independent project while seeking relevant employment.
3. Delay the move because the remaining route does not fit her current time or income constraints.

She chooses based on access and affordability. She does not automatically move the year-two milestone forward because the calendar says year one has ended.

## Give the roadmap explicit branches

Write a branch where you can already see an important uncertainty.

| Situation | Adjustment |
| --- | --- |
| The work interests me, but quality is below the required standard | Practise the specific weakness and obtain another review |
| I can perform the tasks, but the typical working conditions are unacceptable | Investigate another setting or a different task mix |
| Required experience is unavailable in my current role | Seek another assignment, a suitable external opportunity, or a longer route |
| A formal requirement is unclear | Verify it with the relevant official authority before committing |
| The route exceeds my available time or resources | Reduce scope, extend the timeline, or pause |
| I no longer want the destination after trying representative work | Reconsider the direction and retain evidence that is useful elsewhere |

A backup route should preserve something valuable. It might use the same analytical capabilities in your existing field while you reconsider an industry move. It need not be a second five-year plan developed in equal detail.

England’s National Careers Service advises combining a long-term aim with shorter-term goals, considering different routes, and accounting for personal circumstances. This supports a flexible planning approach; it does not prescribe the stages or timelines in this article. [National Careers Service skills and planning guidance](https://nationalcareers.service.gov.uk/careers-advice/identifying-skills-and-upskilling).

## Copy this roadmap template

Use as many stages as your situation requires. Keep the distant stages brief until experience supports greater detail.

| Stage and approximate period | Responsibility I want to develop | Output or experience | How quality will be checked | Dependency or constraint | Continue, adjust, or stop condition |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Next stage |  |  |  |  |  |
| Following stage |  |  |  |  |  |
| Longer-term possibility |  |  |  |  |  |

Below the table, add:

> **My direction:**  
> **The most important assumption:**  
> **The next action I can take:**  
> **The alternative if the main route becomes unavailable:**  
> **The next review date or event:**

Review after a meaningful project, a change in circumstances, or new information about requirements. A regular calendar reminder can help, but do not wait for it when a critical dependency has changed.

## Make the first commitment smaller than the destination

Before committing to an expensive programme or a major move, identify what you still need to learn. You might first need a representative task, a discussion about project access, or confirmation of an entry requirement.

Use [Annual Career Review System](/en/career/guides/annual-career-review-system) if you need to establish your starting evidence. Use [Build a Portfolio for Career Switching](/en/career/guides/build-portfolio-for-career-switch) when the next stage requires a work sample. If the route changes industries, [Cross-Industry Move Strategy](/en/career/guides/cross-industry-move-strategy) helps separate transferable tasks from knowledge you still need.

The [career guides library](/en/career/guides) provides other routes into the planning process.

Your next action should make the roadmap better informed. It does not have to make the next five years certain.

snapshot.title: Build a Portfolio for Career Switching
snapshot.excerpt: Build work samples around the tasks your target role requires. Show your decisions, contribution, checks, and limitations—with a complete fictional example you can follow.
snapshot.body_md:
# Build a Portfolio for Career Switching

A career-change portfolio should help someone examine how you approach work relevant to the role you want.

A polished final screen or document may show presentation quality. To demonstrate judgment, include the question you addressed, the materials available, the choices you made, and the checks you performed.

You can build this evidence through authorised work, independent projects, or clearly labelled simulations. Each supports different claims. A simulation can show your approach to a task; it cannot establish that an employer adopted your work or that it produced a business result.

## Begin with the hiring question

Choose a target role and identify the tasks you need to demonstrate. Use the actual role description, relevant official occupational information, and any portfolio instructions from the employer.

Translate broad requirements into observable work:

| Broad requirement | More useful evidence question |
| --- | --- |
| Analytical ability | Can this person turn imperfect information into a defensible answer? |
| Communication | Can the intended audience understand the conclusion and act on it? |
| Project coordination | Can this person identify dependencies, responsibilities, and unresolved issues? |
| Design judgment | Can this person explain choices in relation to users, constraints, and alternatives? |
| Technical skill | Does the work function, and can the person explain its behaviour and limitations? |

Do not build a separate project for every phrase in a vacancy. Select material that answers an important question well.

CareerOneStop recommends including work samples with descriptions of the project, your contribution, and results. It also advises keeping the collection manageable and checking its presentation and links. This is practical US job-search guidance, not evidence that a particular portfolio will secure an offer. [CareerOneStop portfolio guidance](https://cloudfront.careeronestop.org/JobSearch/Resumes/portfolios.aspx).

## Choose material you can honestly explain and share

For an existing project, establish what you are permitted to disclose before building the case around it. Removing names or changing numbers does not automatically make employer or client material available for reuse.

If sharing permission is unclear, choose another sample or create an original simulation without copying restricted inputs. Label a reconstruction as a reconstruction and explain what was changed.

Use precise contribution statements:

- “I wrote the analysis and prepared the recommendation; another team member collected the data.”
- “I implemented these components within a team project.”
- “This is an independent exercise using synthetic information. It was not commissioned or deployed.”

A result also needs a boundary. “The client approved the recommendation” differs from “The recommendation increased retention.” Claim only what the evidence supports.

## A complete worked sample: checking event registration data

The following is a fictional teaching example. Leo, the assignment, every record, the review comments, and the conclusions are invented. It demonstrates a portfolio case structure, not a real client engagement or hiring outcome.

Leo is an administrative coordinator exploring operations analyst roles. He wants a sample that shows how he checks data and communicates uncertainty.

### The brief

A fictional event organiser asks:

> How many confirmed registrations are in this export, and what still needs checking before we give a planning number to the event team?

Leo defines the task narrowly. He will reconcile registrations in a single snapshot. He will not predict attendance or claim to know how many people will arrive.

### The materials

He creates this synthetic CSV. The repeated names are intentional; all names are invented.

```csv
registration_id,display_name,status
R01,Ari,confirmed
R02,Sam,confirmed
R03,Jo,cancelled
R02,Sam,confirmed
R04,Priya,
R05,Alex,confirmed
R01,Ari,confirmed
R06,Alex,cancelled
R07,Mei,confirmed
R08,Noor,
R05,Alex,confirmed
R09,Luis,confirmed
```

He includes the CSV in the sample so that a reviewer can reproduce the checks. He also states an assumption: within this exercise, the registration ID identifies a registration, and repeated rows with the same ID and identical values are duplicate exports.

That assumption would need verification with the data owner in a real assignment. If one ID contained conflicting statuses, simply keeping the first row would not resolve the conflict.

### First approach and the error it reveals

Leo initially tries removing duplicates by display name. This would combine the two records named Alex even though they have different registration IDs and statuses.

He records why the method is unsuitable: a shared name does not establish a shared registration. He changes the duplicate rule to use the stated identifier and checks whether repeated IDs contain conflicting values.

This correction belongs in the case. It shows how he identified and revised a weak decision.

### Reconciliation

The sample contains twelve rows. R01, R02, and R05 each have one additional identical row, leaving nine distinct registration IDs.

The unique records reconcile as follows:

| Check | Result |
| --- | --- |
| Raw export rows | 12 |
| Additional identical rows removed | 3 |
| Unique registration IDs | 9 |
| Confirmed | 5 |
| Cancelled | 2 |
| Missing status | 2 |
| Status reconciliation | 5 + 2 + 2 = 9 |

Leo treats missing status as unknown. He does not silently recode it as confirmed or cancelled.

The confirmed records are R01, R02, R05, R07, and R09. R03 and R06 are cancelled. R04 and R08 need clarification.

### The decision note

His final note reads:

> This synthetic snapshot contains five confirmed registrations after removing three additional identical rows. Two registrations are cancelled and two have no status. If both unknown records are later confirmed, the confirmed count would become seven. This is a range of possible registration statuses, not an attendance forecast. Confirm the two missing statuses and the meaning of the identifier before using the result operationally.

The note answers the brief and makes the remaining decision visible.

It avoids an unsupported “improvement” claim. Leo has not saved a real organisation money or improved an actual event. He has demonstrated a checking process on a deliberately small dataset.

### Review and revision

In the fictional review, a reader asks, “Why is seven not your forecast?”

Leo revises the heading from “Expected attendance” to “Registration status reconciliation” and places the explanation beside the table. He also adds a note that different IDs may represent separate registrations by the same person; determining unique people would require another definition and appropriate information.

The revision improves the accuracy of the sample’s claim. It does not make the dataset more realistic than it is.

### What this case demonstrates

The sample gives a reviewer evidence of problem definition, identifier checking, reconciliation, handling missing information, and explaining a conclusion.

It leaves other questions open. It does not show Leo working with large datasets, combining multiple systems, operating under workplace pressure, or obtaining stakeholder agreement. He should describe those as gaps or provide other evidence where the target role requires them.

## Build the case around the evidence chain

For your own sample, copy this structure:

| Case element | What the reader needs |
| --- | --- |
| Brief | The question, audience, and intended decision |
| Inputs | What information or materials were available and their source |
| Constraints | Time, scope, permissions, tools, and known limitations |
| Contribution | What you personally did and what others did |
| Decisions | Choices you made, alternatives considered, and reasons |
| Checks | How you examined accuracy, function, or usability |
| Output | The actual sample, not only a description of it |
| Result | What happened, or what the exercise established |
| Revision | Feedback or a problem that changed the work |
| Boundary | What the sample cannot demonstrate |

Give the reader a short route through the case, with supporting material available where it adds value. A concise introduction can state the task and strongest evidence; the fuller version can show decisions and checks.

The US Office of Personnel Management describes work-sample assessments as tasks that resemble job activities, evaluated under defined conditions. A self-selected portfolio is a different form of evidence. Its quality depends on what the reviewer can inspect; it does not inherit the validity of a structured hiring assessment. [OPM work samples and simulations](https://www.opm.gov/policy-data-oversight/assessment-and-selection/other-assessment-methods/work-samples-and-simulations/).

## Review the sample before adding more projects

Ask a suitable reader to examine a specific question: “Can you follow why I excluded these records?” or “Which required capability remains unsupported?” General approval is less informative.

Use the response to decide what comes next:

| Observation | Useful response |
| --- | --- |
| The method contains a substantive error | Correct it and explain the revised reasoning before sharing |
| The work is sound, but the contribution is unclear | Identify ownership beside the relevant output |
| The reader cannot find the evidence | Improve navigation and remove unnecessary material |
| The sample answers a different task from the target role | Rework the brief or choose a more relevant sample |
| Sharing permission is unresolved | Stop sharing that material; use an authorised alternative |
| A role requires experience the sample cannot show | Acknowledge the gap and investigate how to obtain it |

Low response to applications does not establish which part of the portfolio is wrong. Role requirements, eligibility, the application, and other factors may matter. Look for specific evidence before repeatedly redesigning the presentation.

Interest questionnaires cannot fill an evidence gap. If you keep an interest report alongside your planning, the [RIASEC PDF and download guidance](/en/holland-test/pdf-download) addresses report-related questions; the portfolio itself should show relevant work.

When you have a sample, use it to refine your [five-year career roadmap](/en/career/guides/build-five-year-career-roadmap). If the difficulty is transferring experience into another sector, use [Cross-Industry Move Strategy](/en/career/guides/cross-industry-move-strategy). You can find other resources in the [career guides library](/en/career/guides).

Before sending the portfolio, check that the files open, the links work, the content is readable, and every claim matches the evidence provided.

before.title: Cross-Industry Move Strategy
before.excerpt: Actionable framework to improve decision quality and execution in career development.
before.body_md:
# Cross-Industry Move Strategy

## Why This Matters
Career growth is a compound system. Better decisions early reduce switching costs and improve long-term optionality.

## Practical Framework
1. Define one 12-month target role with explicit success criteria.
2. Build a capability backlog across knowledge, projects, and collaboration behavior.
3. Run 4-week execution sprints and collect measurable evidence.
4. Review outcomes quarterly and adjust strategy using market and fit signals.

## Implementation Checklist
- Clear role target and industry context
- Evidence-based skill gap map
- Portfolio or project proof
- Feedback loop with mentors and stakeholders

snapshot.title: Cross-Industry Move Strategy
snapshot.excerpt: Compare the tasks you can already demonstrate with the domain knowledge, requirements, and working conditions of a new industry. Choose a realistic entry route and test its weakest assumption.
snapshot.body_md:
# Cross-Industry Move Strategy

A cross-industry move requires two connected judgments: what your previous work enables you to do, and what you still need to learn in the new setting.

Experience does not become irrelevant when the industry changes. It also does not transfer automatically because two jobs use similar words.

Start with the target work. Identify the tasks, the context in which they happen, and the consequences of getting them wrong. Then compare those demands with evidence from your own experience.

## Separate industry, role, and working conditions

Write what you want to change and what you hope to retain.

You might want to leave an industry while continuing project coordination. You might want to change functions while remaining in a familiar sector. Or the problem may concern one employer’s staffing, schedule, or management arrangements.

These lead to different searches.

| Question | Why it changes the plan |
| --- | --- |
| Which industry or customer context do I want to enter? | Identifies the knowledge and relationships to investigate |
| Which tasks do I want to perform? | Defines what experience could transfer |
| Which responsibilities am I ready to hold? | Helps distinguish an appropriate entry point from a title aspiration |
| Which working conditions can I accept? | Tests whether the route is feasible |
| What am I trying to leave behind? | Helps check whether the target actually changes that condition |

A move into a new industry may still involve the same disliked tasks. Check the ordinary work as carefully as the sector’s reputation.

Australia’s myGov guidance connects career change with existing skills and qualifications, identifying gaps, and investigating further training where needed. Its service links are Australian; the underlying planning distinction is between what you bring and what the target requires. [myGov career-change guidance](https://my.gov.au/en/services/education/upgrading-professional-skills-or-qualifications/changing-your-career).

## Map tasks with their context attached

Replace “I am good at stakeholder management” with an example of what you did.

For each relevant task, record:

1. The problem and people involved.
2. Your action and level of responsibility.
3. The constraints under which you worked.
4. The output and available evidence.
5. What would be different in the target setting.

For example, coordinating a store opening may demonstrate scheduling dependencies and escalating delays. It does not by itself demonstrate the ability to configure a software platform, interpret a clinical workflow, or approve a technical design.

Use three categories:

| Category | Meaning | Next action |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Demonstrated and relevant | You have evidence of a task substantially similar to the target task | Explain the evidence in terms the target audience understands |
| Relevant with adaptation | Part of the task transfers, but tools, customers, scale, or processes differ | Identify and practise the changed part |
| Not yet demonstrated | You lack evidence or the necessary knowledge | Investigate training, supervised experience, or another route |

Avoid scoring the categories into a single “fit percentage.” One unresolved requirement can matter more than several areas of overlap.

## Distinguish knowledge gaps from entry requirements

Some gaps can be explored through an introductory project. Others require a formal route.

A task may depend on:

- Knowing the customer’s workflow and terminology.
- Understanding how the organisation measures performance.
- Using a specific tool or technical method.
- Following an approval, safety, or compliance process.
- Holding a required qualification, registration, or authorisation.

Check formal requirements with the responsible regulator or official authority for the exact role and location. A vacancy or practitioner conversation can identify a question to investigate; it does not settle a legal requirement.

Similarly, an adjacent role is not automatically an easier route. It may have different requirements. Compare the actual responsibilities, training, and conditions.

## Worked example: retail operations to software implementation

The following is a fictional teaching example. Amira, the role descriptions, practitioners, exercises, and feedback are invented. They do not describe current vacancies or typical hiring outcomes.

Amira coordinates changes across retail stores. She wants to work for a company supplying inventory software to retailers.

She initially describes her experience as “running complex implementations.” When she examines a fictional target role, she sees that implementation includes customer discovery, data mapping, system setup, testing, and user training.

Her retail experience overlaps with some of that work:

| Target task in the fictional role | Amira’s existing evidence | What remains unproven |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Coordinate rollout activities | A store change schedule and dependency record | Managing the supplier’s software delivery process |
| Explain a changed workflow | Training notes she created for store teams | Teaching users to complete tasks in the target product |
| Investigate customer needs | Examples of clarifying store operating problems | Running discovery across unfamiliar client systems |
| Map inventory data | Experience checking store records | Field definitions, import rules, and validation in the software |
| Approve technical setup | No relevant evidence | Required technical knowledge and decision authority |

She can present the coordination evidence without claiming competence across the whole implementation.

### Choose the uncertainty that could change the route

Amira considers a customer onboarding coordinator role and a more technical implementation role.

The main uncertainty is whether she wants—and can develop—the data and configuration work required for the technical route. Reading more general articles about the software industry would not answer it.

She creates an independent exercise using synthetic store information. It contains product identifiers, store identifiers, units of measure, and stock quantities. The brief asks her to propose how the information should be checked before a hypothetical import.

She prepares a field-definition table, lists ambiguous records, and distinguishes issues she can resolve from questions requiring a product specialist.

This exercise is not a test of any real product and does not establish that she can configure it.

### Observe the gap and revise the plan

In the fictional review, a practitioner points out that Amira treats “quantity” as though every record uses the same unit. Some records refer to individual items and others to boxes.

Amira uses the existing unit field to check each quantity, documents the conversion assumption, and flags cases without a known conversion rather than silently converting them.

The observation changes her learning plan. She now needs to understand data definitions and validation, rather than merely learning industry vocabulary.

She also notices that she enjoys explaining customer workflows more than investigating technical setup. She keeps the technical route open but prioritises roles whose actual responsibilities emphasise coordination and user support, checking their requirements individually.

### Set a condition for proceeding

Amira’s next decision depends on the evidence:

- If she can explain the workflow and data checks, and a role provides training for the remaining product knowledge, she can consider applying.
- If a role expects independent technical configuration that she cannot demonstrate, she needs further preparation or a different entry point.
- If the role’s schedule conflicts with her circumstances, she excludes it even if the tasks are attractive.
- If she discovers a required qualification or authorisation, she verifies the official route before committing.

The exercise has narrowed the uncertainty. It has not produced a claim that she is “industry ready.”

## Build the entry route around the remaining gap

Choose a route for a reason.

**A similar function in another industry** may let you reuse stronger evidence while learning a new context. Check whether the new setting changes the task substantially.

**A role connecting familiar customers with a new product** may make your customer knowledge relevant. Check the product, technical, and commercial responsibilities.

**A supervised or trainee route** may be appropriate when the organisation explicitly provides training. Confirm what is taught and what is expected at entry.

**A formal training route** may be necessary where the profession or employer requires it. Verify requirements and recognition locally before paying for a programme.

**An internal cross-sector project** can provide experience when available and authorised. Do not assume your current employer can offer it.

NSW Government’s career-change guidance recommends examining transferable skills, talking to people doing the work, and considering financial, family, and location constraints. These are useful investigation topics, not a guarantee that a transition is feasible. [NSW career-change first steps](https://www.nsw.gov.au/employment/my-career-planner/getting-a-job/changing-careers/first-steps).

## Copy this transition checklist

Before investing heavily or committing to a move, complete the questions relevant to your route:

- [ ] I can describe the target’s recurring tasks, rather than only its industry label.
- [ ] I have examples showing which tasks I can already perform.
- [ ] I have stated where the context changes the task.
- [ ] I know which knowledge gaps matter most at entry.
- [ ] I have checked formal requirements with the relevant official authority where applicable.
- [ ] I understand what training the specific opportunity actually provides.
- [ ] I have investigated schedule, location, travel, and other conditions that matter to me.
- [ ] I can explain the practical cost and timing of the route.
- [ ] I have identified the uncertainty that would change my decision.
- [ ] I have a next action and a condition for reconsidering.

An unchecked item is a question to resolve, not an automatic rejection. Prioritise the item that could make the move infeasible.

## When to adjust or stop

If feedback repeatedly identifies the same missing capability, address it directly or choose a role requiring a different level of readiness.

If your examples use unfamiliar language, explain the underlying work plainly. Do not replace old jargon with new jargon you cannot explain.

If you cannot obtain a representative task or credible information, limit the commitment until you understand what you are entering.

If the ordinary work remains unappealing after you investigate it, reconsider the destination. Attraction to an industry’s mission does not require you to pursue every role within it.

If your evidence is useful but poorly presented, use [Build a Portfolio for Career Switching](/en/career/guides/build-portfolio-for-career-switch). If the route requires several stages, use [Build a Five-Year Career Roadmap](/en/career/guides/build-five-year-career-roadmap). The [career guides library](/en/career/guides) provides related planning resources.

An interest report can help you notice activities you want to explore. For report-related questions, see the [RIASEC PDF and download guidance](/en/holland-test/pdf-download). Keep those interests alongside evidence of skills and the target’s actual requirements. A test cannot decide the move for you.
